rows.notes: The simplest if/else. Anchors the family: a failure here means the whole control lane is wrong.
Else arm of the same template.
An if with no else emits nothing, not an empty-string placeholder.

rows.source: {% if n == 1 %}one{% elif n == 2 %}two{% elif n == 3 %}three{% else %}many{% endif %}
rows.notes: elif chain, middle arm.

rows.source: {% if n == 1 %}one{% elif n == 2 %}two{% elif n == 3 %}three{% else %}many{% endif %}
rows.notes: elif chain, last arm before else.

rows.source: {% if n == 1 %}one{% elif n == 2 %}two{% elif n == 3 %}three{% else %}many{% endif %}
rows.notes: elif chain falling through to else.

rows.source: {% if a %}A{% if b %}B{% else %}b{% endif %}{% else %}x{% endif %}
rows.notes: Nested if inside the taken arm of an outer if.
Statement-level truthiness of the empty string.
Statement-level truthiness of integer zero.
Statement-level truthiness of an empty sequence.
Statement-level truthiness of an empty mapping.
Statement-level truthiness of none.
An undefined name in a condition is falsy under the default (lenient) undefined behaviour rather than an error.
Attribute access chained off an undefined value inside a condition: whether the statement swallows it or raises.
Inline conditional expression, the interpolation-level counterpart of the if statement.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ x }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Anchor row for the for family.

rows.source: [{% for x in xs %}{{ x }}{% endfor %}]
rows.notes: An empty sequence emits the loop body zero times.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ x }}{% else %}empty{% endfor %}
rows.notes: for/else with an empty sequence runs the else body.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ x }}{% else %}empty{% endfor %}
rows.notes: for/else with a non-empty sequence must not run the else body.

rows.source: {% for x in xs if x > 1 %}{{ x }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Filtered for loop. Rust compiles it as an accumulating inner loop plus a normal outer loop (codegen.rs compile_for_loop).

rows.source: {% for x in xs if x > 5 %}{{ x }}{% else %}none{% endfor %}
rows.notes: A filter that rejects everything must still reach the else body.

rows.source: {% for a, b in xs %}{{ a }}-{{ b }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Target-list unpacking in a for statement.

rows.source: {% for a, b in xs %}{{ a }}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Unpacking a 3-element item into 2 targets. Rust has a dedicated CannotUnpack kind; this row pins what the fork reports.

rows.source: {% for c in s %}{{ c }}.{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Iterating a string yields characters.

rows.source: {% for k in m %}{{ k }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Iterating a mapping yields keys. Insertion order is alphabetical here on purpose, so this row isolates iteration from the known preserve_order divergence (container/map-loop-insertion-order).

rows.source: {% for k, v in m|items %}{{ k }}={{ v }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Unpacking pairs out of |items. Alphabetical insertion order for the same reason as the previous row.

rows.source: {% for i in range(3) %}{{ i }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Iterating a lazily produced sequence rather than a materialized list.
Iterating a non-iterable. Error category, not bytes.

rows.source: [{% for x in missing %}{{ x }}{% endfor %}]
rows.notes: Iterating an undefined name under default undefined behaviour.

rows.source: [{% for x in v %}{{ x }}{% endfor %}]
rows.notes: Iterating none, which is a different value from undefined.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{% for y in xs %}{{ x }}{{ y }} {% endfor %}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Nested loops over the same sequence: the inner loop must not disturb the outer iterator.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{% endfor %}[{{ x }}]
rows.notes: The loop target must not leak out of the loop frame.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop.index }}/{{ loop.index0 }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: loop.index / loop.index0.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop.revindex }}/{{ loop.revindex0 }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: loop.revindex / loop.revindex0, which Rust computes with saturating subtraction.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop.first }},{{ loop.last }},{{ loop.length }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: loop.first / loop.last / loop.length, including the rendered spelling of the booleans.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop.first }}{{ loop.last }}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: A one-item loop is both first and last.

rows.source: {% for i in range(3) %}[{{ loop.length }},{{ loop.revindex }},{{ loop.last }}]{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Rust derives loop.length from an exact size hint and returns undefined when there is none (loop_object.rs). This row pins what a range-backed loop reports.

rows.source: {% for x in xs if x > 1 %}{{ loop.length }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: A filtered loop iterates an accumulated list, so its length is the post-filter count.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{% for y in xs %}{{ loop.depth }}{{ loop.depth0 }};{% endfor %}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: loop.depth / loop.depth0 in a nested (non-recursive) loop: nesting alone does not increase depth in minijinja.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}[{{ loop.previtem }}|{{ x }}|{{ loop.nextitem }}]{% endfor %}
rows.notes: adjacent_loop_items is one of BAML's enabled engine features. previtem/nextitem are undefined at the edges and undefined renders as empty.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop.nextitem }}:{{ x }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Reading nextitem pulls from the underlying iterator; the peeked item must still be produced by the loop itself.

rows.source: {% for i in range(3) %}[{{ loop.previtem }}|{{ i }}|{{ loop.nextitem }}]{% endfor %}
rows.notes: The same adjacency machinery over a lazy iterator rather than a list.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop.cycle('a','b') }}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: loop.cycle over two values across four iterations.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop.cycle() }}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Adversarial: Rust computes idx % args.len() before checking the argument list (loop_object.rs call_method), so an empty argument list is a remainder-by-zero. A panic is an outcome here, not a crashed run.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop.changed(x) }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: loop.changed remembers the previous argument tuple across iterations.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop.changed(x, 1) }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: loop.changed compares the whole argument tuple, not just the first argument.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop.nope() }}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: The loop object answers exactly two methods; anything else is an unknown-method error in Rust.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Rust renders the loop object as `<loop idx/len>` (loop_object.rs render). Rendered bytes, so this is a prompt-visible surface.
`loop` is a reserved name but is only bound inside a loop frame.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{% for y in xs %}{{ loop.index }}{% endfor %}{{ loop.index }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: The inner loop shadows `loop` and the outer binding must be restored when the inner frame pops.

rows.source: {% for item in tree recursive %}{{ item.name }}({{ loop.depth }}){% if item.children %}[{{ loop(item.children) }}]{% endif %};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Recursive for loop driven by loop(...), including loop.depth at each level. Map keys are alphabetical so this row does not double as an ordering probe.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop(xs) }}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Calling loop() in a loop that was not declared recursive.
Anchor row for set.
Reassignment reading the previous binding.
Unpacking assignment outside a loop.
Block form of set captures the rendered body.

rows.source: {% set x | trim %}   padded   {% endset %}[{{ x }}]
rows.notes: Block set with a filter applied to the captured body.

rows.source: {% set x = 1 %}{% if true %}{% set x = 2 %}{% endif %}{{ x }}
rows.notes: An if statement does not open a new assignment scope.

rows.source: {% set x = 0 %}{% for i in xs %}{% set x = i %}{% endfor %}{{ x }}
rows.notes: The classic Jinja scoping rule: a set inside a loop frame does not survive the loop.

rows.source: {% set ns = namespace(total=0) %}{% for i in xs %}{% set ns.total = ns.total + i %}{% endfor %}{{ ns.total }}
rows.notes: The documented way to accumulate across a loop frame: dotted set on a namespace object.
Dotted assignment onto a non-namespace object.
RESERVED_NAMES rejects assignment to loop/self/true/false/none at parse time.
with opens a scope that its bindings do not outlive.

rows.source: {% set x = 1 %}{% with x = 2 %}{{ x }}{% endwith %}{{ x }}
rows.notes: with shadows an outer binding and restores it.
filter block applies a filter to its rendered body.
filter block with filter arguments.
Unknown filter reached through the block form rather than the pipe form.
The autoescape statement switches escaping on inside a .txt template, whose default is none.
Explicitly disabling autoescape, and the state afterwards.
Escaping state must be restored when the block ends.
do evaluates and discards. Unlike include/extends, it is not gated behind multi_template.

rows.source: {% set ns = namespace(v=1) %}{% do ns %}{{ ns.v }}
rows.notes: do with a bare expression that has no output.
A comment contributes no bytes.
Without trim markers the whitespace around a comment survives.
Explicit trim markers on a comment.

rows.source:
a
{# line one
line two #}
b
rows.notes: A comment spanning lines: the newlines around it are template data.
Statement and interpolation syntax inside a comment is inert.
Unterminated comment.
raw emits its body verbatim, including things that would otherwise be syntax.
raw is byte-preserving in the default whitespace configuration.
Trim markers on both raw delimiters. Rust applies trim_start/trim_end to the raw body itself (lexer.rs).
Unterminated raw block: a lexer-level syntax error.
A tag that merely starts with endraw must not close the raw block.
Anchor row for macros, which BAML enables and relies on for template-string injection.

rows.source: {% macro greet(name, punct='!') %}{{ name }}{{ punct }}{% endmacro %}{{ greet('a') }}{{ greet('b', '?') }}
rows.notes: Default argument used and overridden.

rows.source: {% macro m(a, b) %}{{ a }}-{{ b }}{% endmacro %}{{ m(b=2, a=1) }}
rows.notes: Keyword arguments out of positional order.
A macro argument that is not supplied is undefined rather than an error (macro_object.rs fills Value::UNDEFINED).
More positional arguments than the macro declares.

rows.source: {% macro m(a) %}{{ a }}{% endmacro %}{{ m(1, nope=2) }}
rows.notes: Rust reports an unknown keyword argument as TooManyArguments.

rows.source: {% macro m(a) %}{{ a }}{% endmacro %}{{ m(1, a=2) }}
rows.notes: The same argument supplied positionally and by keyword.
Rust renders a macro value as `<macro name>` (macro_object.rs render).
The macro object exposes name/arguments/caller.
The argument-name list, including how a sequence of strings renders.
caller is false for a macro that does not reference caller().
Referencing caller() in the body flips the macro's caller flag at compile time (codegen.rs).

rows.source: {% set outer = 'O' %}{% macro m() %}{{ outer }}{% endmacro %}{{ m() }}
rows.notes: A macro closes over the enclosing scope at definition time.

rows.source: {% set v = 'first' %}{% macro m() %}{{ v }}{% endmacro %}{% set v = 'second' %}{{ m() }}
rows.notes: Whether the closure sees the value at definition time or at call time.

rows.source: {% macro count(n) %}{{ n }}{% if n > 1 %}{{ count(n - 1) }}{% endif %}{% endmacro %}{{ count(3) }}
rows.notes: A macro that calls itself.

rows.source: {% macro row(i, v) %}{{ i }}:{{ v }};{% endmacro %}{% for x in xs %}{{ row(loop.index, x) }}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Macro invoked from inside a loop frame, taking loop metadata as an argument. This is the shape BAML's injected template-string macros are used in.

rows.source: {% macro inner(x) %}<{{ x }}>{% endmacro %}{% macro outer(x) %}[{{ inner(x) }}]{% endmacro %}{{ outer('v') }}
rows.notes: A macro calling another macro defined earlier in the same template.

rows.source: {% macro outer(x) %}[{{ inner(x) }}]{% endmacro %}{% macro inner(x) %}<{{ x }}>{% endmacro %}{{ outer('v') }}
rows.notes: A macro referring to one defined after it: whether the closure resolves late.

rows.source: {% if true %}{% macro m() %}in-if{% endmacro %}{% endif %}{{ m() }}
rows.notes: Macro defined inside a conditional branch and called outside it.
A macro body's leading/trailing newlines are part of its output in the default whitespace configuration.

rows.source: {% macro wrap() %}[{{ caller() }}]{% endmacro %}{% call wrap() %}inner{% endcall %}
rows.notes: call block: the body becomes the macro's caller().

rows.source: {% macro each(xs) %}{% for x in xs %}{{ caller(x, loop.index) }}{% endfor %}{% endmacro %}{% call(v, i) each(xs) %}{{ i }}={{ v }};{% endcall %}
rows.notes: call with its own parameter list, invoked repeatedly from inside the macro.

rows.source: {% macro wrap(tag) %}<{{ tag }}>{{ caller() }}</{{ tag }}>{% endmacro %}{% call wrap('b') %}x{% endcall %}
rows.notes: call block where the macro itself also takes arguments.

rows.source: {% macro wrap(c) %}({{ c }}:{{ caller() }}){% endmacro %}{% call wrap('outer') %}{% call wrap('inner') %}x{% endcall %}{% endcall %}
rows.notes: Nested call blocks: the inner caller must not clobber the outer one.
A macro that references caller() but is invoked without a call block.
caller() at top level, where no macro frame supplies it.
Prompt-shaped macro library: several macros defined then composed, which is how BAML's injected template-string macros are consumed.

NEGATIVE CONTROL. BAML builds the engine without multi_template, so `include` is not a statement at all: the parser reports `unknown statement include` (parser.rs parse_stmt_unprotected). The fork must not resolve or load anything here.
NEGATIVE CONTROL. The ignore-missing form must not silently succeed either.
NEGATIVE CONTROL. Template inheritance is unavailable without multi_template.
NEGATIVE CONTROL. Module import is unavailable without multi_template.
NEGATIVE CONTROL. from-import is unavailable without multi_template.
NEGATIVE CONTROL. `block` is gated behind multi_template too, so even a self-contained block is a syntax error.
NEGATIVE CONTROL. super() inside a block, which cannot exist without multi_template.
NEGATIVE CONTROL. super() is compiled unconditionally (codegen.rs FastSuper) but has no block to super into.
NEGATIVE CONTROL. The self/block call form is only compiled with multi_template; without it this is an ordinary attribute call.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{% break %}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: NEGATIVE CONTROL. loop_controls is not among BAML's features, so `break` is an unknown statement.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{% continue %}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: NEGATIVE CONTROL. Same for `continue`.
NEGATIVE CONTROL. A closing tag for a statement the engine does not have.
Unclosed if. Pins that a compile failure is classifiable by an external consumer.
Unclosed for.
Unclosed macro.
A closing tag with no opening statement.
Closing an if with endfor.

rows.source: {% if a %}1{% else %}2{% elif b %}3{% endif %}
rows.notes: elif after else.
Two else arms.
An identifier that is not a statement keyword.
An empty statement tag.
A non-identifier where a block keyword is expected.
Unterminated interpolation.
Unterminated statement tag.
An interpolation with no expression.
Unterminated string literal inside an interpolation.
for with neither target nor iterable.
for with a missing `in` keyword.
set with an empty right-hand side.
A stray endset.
A stray endcall.
A call block naming something that is not a macro.
Calling a name that is not bound: the runtime counterpart of the syntax rows above.
Unclosed filter block.
Unclosed with block.
Unclosed autoescape block.
The whitespace baseline: no trim_blocks, no lstrip_blocks, no keep_trailing_newline. Every newline around the tags is template data, and the final newline is stripped at tokenizer construction.
trim_blocks eats the first newline after a block tag (lexer.rs skip_newline_if_trim_blocks).
lstrip_blocks removes horizontal whitespace before a block tag that starts a line.
Both flags together: the configuration BAML's own environment sets (jinja_helpers.rs). The engine machinery is what is being compared here.
lstrip_blocks deliberately does not apply to interpolations (should_lstrip_block excludes StartMarker::Variable).
A tag with non-whitespace earlier on the line is not lstripped.
Start of file counts as start of line for lstrip_blocks.
trim_blocks with CRLF line endings: Rust skips a \r and then a \n.
The same CRLF template without trim_blocks: every CR and LF is template data.
A left trim marker removes preceding whitespace including newlines.
A right trim marker removes following whitespace.

rows.source: a  {%- if true -%}  b  {%- endif -%}  c
rows.notes: Trim markers on every delimiter of a statement pair.
Trim markers on an interpolation rather than a statement.
An explicit + marker preserves the newline trim_blocks would have eaten.
An explicit + marker preserves the indentation lstrip_blocks would have removed.
With trim_blocks on, a - marker still trims all following whitespace, not just one newline.
The default configuration strips one trailing newline from the source.
keep_trailing_newline preserves it.
Rust strips a trailing \n and then a trailing \r, so a CRLF-terminated template loses both.
Only one trailing newline is stripped.
Comments participate in lstrip_blocks and trim_blocks like statements do.
trim_blocks applies to the raw delimiters, and Rust implements that inside the raw scanner itself.
lstrip_blocks trims the indentation before {% endraw %} out of the raw body.
Rust trims with char::is_whitespace, which includes U+00A0. An ASCII-only trim leaves the byte in the output, so this row is a byte-level probe of the trim character class.
The same character class question on the trailing side, which Rust implements with skip_whitespace over chars.
U+000B VERTICAL TAB is whitespace to Rust's trim_end but not to an ASCII space/tab/CR/LF set.
U+000C FORM FEED on the trailing side.
lstrip_blocks with a non-ASCII whitespace character in the indentation: Rust's lstrip_block trims any whitespace that is not a newline.
The raw scanner uses trim_start/trim_end on the raw body, so it has the same character-class question.
A realistic prompt-shaped template under BAML's whitespace configuration: indentation, loop, branch and blank-line handling all at once. Map keys are alphabetical so ordering is not a variable here.
Macro output composed inside a loop under trim/lstrip: the exact newline count is the thing being pinned.
Unpacking arity is checked outside a for loop too: Rust compiles both through the same UnpackList instruction.
Unpacking something that cannot be iterated at all.
Dotted assignment onto an undefined name, the other half of the namespace-only assignment rule.

rows.source: {% with a, b = xs %}{{ a }}{{ b }}{% endwith %}
rows.notes: Whether a with block accepts a target list at all, and with what result.
A bound value that is not callable is a different error from an unbound name (vm/mod.rs CallFunction).
Bound to undefined rather than unbound: Rust reports 'value of type undefined is not callable'.

rows.source: {% macro m() %}x{% endmacro %}{% call m() %}body{% endcall %}
rows.notes: A call block against a macro that never references caller(). Rust passes caller as a keyword argument, so the macro rejects it as an unknown keyword argument.
caller supplied by hand as a keyword argument: accepted as an argument because the macro references caller, then not callable.
The form of do that is actually valid: Rust requires a call expression (parser.rs parse_do).

rows.source: {% for item in tree recursive %}{{ loop.depth }}{% for c in pair %}{{ loop.depth }}{% endfor %}{% if item.children %}{{ loop(item.children) }}{% endif %}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: A plain loop nested inside a recursive one. Rust advances the depth counter whenever the ENCLOSING loop is recursive, regardless of whether the inner one is (vm/mod.rs push_loop).

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{% for y in ys %}{{ loop.changed(y) }},{% endfor %};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: changed() state belongs to one loop object: the inner loop starts fresh on each outer iteration.

rows.source: {% for x in xs %}{{ loop.cycle('a','b','c') }}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: cycle indexes by the loop counter, so it wraps rather than tracking call count.

rows.source: {% macro inner(xs) %}{% for x in xs %}{{ loop.depth }}{{ loop.depth0 }}{% endfor %}{% endmacro %}{% for item in tree recursive %}{{ inner(pair) }}{% if item.children %}{{ loop(item.children) }}{% endif %}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: A macro called from inside a recursive loop, containing a loop of its own. Rust evaluates a macro body in a fresh state whose context has no current loop, so the inner loop starts at depth 0 no matter how deep the caller is.

rows.source: {% macro peek() %}[{{ loop }}]{% endmacro %}{% for x in xs %}{{ peek() }}{% endfor %}
rows.notes: Whether the caller's loop variable leaks into a macro body.

rows.source: {% macro mark(v) %}{{ v }}{% endmacro %}{% for x in xs %}{{ mark(loop.changed(x)) }};{% endfor %}
rows.notes: changed() evaluated in the caller and passed into a macro: the state belongs to the loop, not to the call.
